item.page_text:
First full-disc image released from MTG-I2 with an animation previewing a service that will update forecasters in Europe every 2.5 minutes
Europe’s meteorological satellite agency, EUMETSAT has released the first image from the Flexible Combined Imager (FCI) on board Meteosat Third Generation Imager 2 (MTG-I2), just over two months after the satellite’s launch on 27 August 2026. The satellite will provide forecasters with high-resolution observations of Europe every 2.5 minutes. This unprecedented frequency will help forecasters monitor fast-developing weather hazards more closely and support earlier, more precise warnings.
Captured from geostationary orbit, some 36,000 km above the Earth, the image acquired on 20 October captures Europe, Africa and the Atlantic in remarkable detail, revealing intricate cloud formations stretching across the North Atlantic, contrasting with the largely clear skies over the Sahara.
While the full-disc image captures a single moment in time, an accompanying rapid-scan animation brings Europe’s weather to life, showing how cloud formations and weather systems evolve through observations taken just 2.5 minutes apart. This offers a glimpse of MTG-I2’s future operational service, which will enable meteorologists to monitor rapidly changing weather conditions over Europe more closely.
These first data follow the handover of MTG-I2 to EUMETSAT’s Mission Control Centre on 9 September, after the successful completion of the Launch and Early Orbit Phase. The satellite is still undergoing calibration and validation, working with the European Space Agency and European industry, to prepare it for operational service, which is expected to begin in the second quarter of 2027.
“This first image, and the animation, is a milestone for EUMETSAT and for our Member States,” EUMETSAT Director-General Phil Evans said. “Just two months after launch, MTG-I2 shows us what rapid scanning will make possible: a much timelier view of fast-developing weather over Europe. As extreme events become more frequent and intense, forecasters and emergency services will be able to see hazards evolve more precisely and act sooner.”
MTG-I2 will empower EUMETSAT’s Member States with a rapid scan service that will deliver high-resolution observations of the European continent every 2.5 minutes. By capturing changes in cloud formations at such rapid intervals, MTG-I2 will help forecasters follow the development of severe weather much more closely. This is especially valuable for fast-developing storms, which can bring heavy rainfall, hail, strong winds and flash floods. Timelier observations will also support earlier, more precise warnings and help emergency response during extreme events, including wildfires.
MTG-I2 is operated by EUMETSAT from its headquarters in Darmstadt, Germany. The satellite was developed by the European Space Agency with Thales Alenia Space as industry prime contractor , fulfilling the requirements set by EUMETSAT in consultation with the meteorological services of its Member States.
Download the high-resolution first full-disc image from MTG-I2 here .
Since 1986, EUMETSAT, Europe’s meteorological satellite agency, has monitored weather and climate from space. From its headquarters in Darmstadt, Germany, it operates a fleet of satellites observing the Earth system and delivers real-time data and imagery to its 30 member states to help protect communities and support critical sectors. Five Meteosat satellites in geostationary orbit provide continuous observations of fast developing weather events, while two polar-orbiting Metop satellites deliver data critical for forecasts up to 10 days ahead. EUMETSAT also supports European sovereignty policies, operating services under the Copernicus programme and leading development and management of the data lake for the Destination Earth initiative.

item.page_text:
The Meteosat Third Generation Imager 2 (MTG-I2) was launched on 27 August 2026. When it is operational - expected in Q2 2027 - it will provide the rapid scan service, which is high resolution imagery of the atmosphere over Europe and North Africa, every two and a half minutes.
This will help meteorologists detect dangerous conditions earlier and track their development in near-real time, providing observations of thunderstorms, dense fog, dust plumes, and much more.
This animation (3-4 November 2026) shows deep convective clouds building over the north-western Sahara as seen from MTG-I2. It starts with true-colour satellite imagery, then transitions to a mix of high-resolution visible and infrared images that make it easier to spot and follow storms and examine their cloud-top features.
The infrared imagery shows cloud-top temperatures and heights, while the visible imagery reveals details of their structure and texture.
These features help forecasters understand how strong a storm is and what its impact might be on the ground.
With this level of detail and a new image every 2.5 minutes, this kind of imagery from MTG-I2 helps forecasters spot and warn of severe weather as it develops.
This animation (2 November 2026) shows Storm Agneta, a deep Mediterranean low, moving over southern Italy on 2 November and bringing heavy rain in its wake.
The combination of high spatial detail and fast imagery from MTG-I2 allows for excellent observation of such storms and their evolution.
Learn more about Meteosat Third Generation satellites

Mythical Tours is a fascinating narrated journey through this imaginary geography, using centuries of historical maps to track down the locations of places that many people today believe exist only in legend.
Among the mythical locations you can discover are the lost city of Atlantis , Hy-Brasil (the phantom island supposedly located off the west coast of Ireland), and even the legendary city of Merlin . item.title: Satellite images show new construction at Iran's missile bases - Vesper
item.summary: Satellite images show new construction at Iran's missile bases. Satellite imagery captured in November shows evidence of digging and new building ...
item.page_text:
Satellite imagery captured in November shows evidence of digging and new building construction near Iranian missile bases. The findings add a fresh indicator of expanding military infrastructure at a time of continued tension between Tehran and Washington.
Satellite imagery reviewed by analysts and taken in November shows continued digging and new building construction in areas near Iranian missile bases. The changes suggest construction activity in the area has accelerated compared with previous months. item.title: U.S. Geological Survey to conduct 'Earth Mapping' flights over NE Iowa, SE Minnesota
item.summary: USGS flight lidar map nov_dec 2026. Map showing the location of the survey [blue polygon] over northeastern Iowa and southeastern Minnesota ...
item.page_text:
RESTON, Va. (KWWL) – Residents in Northeastern Iowa and Southeastern Minnesota may see low-flying airplanes in the months of November and December, and federal officials say there is nothing suspicious and that the aircraft are merely doing "earth mapping" flights to gather important geologic data.
Officials from the U.S. Geological Survey’s Earth Mapping Resources Initiative stated in a press release that the aircraft carry equipment to "image geology" using airborne geophysical technology.
According to a press release, the flights are a collaborative effort between the U.S. Geological Survey’s Earth Mapping Resources Initiative and the Iowa and Minnesota geological surveys.
Jamey Jones, science coordinator for USGS Earth MRI, said the program is called "Earth MRI," and it is the mapping program with a goal to modernize the nation’s maps of geology and mineral resources, and to identify energy and groundwater resources and natural hazards.
“Partnership with state surveys helps accomplish national goals like mapping the critical minerals the U.S. needs. The Iowa and Minnesota geological surveys are helping with the work of the nation -- and adding to state knowledge crucial to water resources, hazards and the resource economy,” Jones stated in a press release.
Robert Tipping, director of the Minnesota Geological Survey, stated that the program, "gives an opportunity to improve our understanding of geologic resources in the state, including materials needed for cleaner sources of energy and national security.
"It accelerates our ongoing mission to provide the geologic information necessary to protect and manage mineral and water resources across the state,” Tipping added.
Ryan Clark, aassociate Iowa state geologist for energy and minerals, was also excited about the study results.
“These new data will greatly enhance our understanding of the potential for critical minerals and geologic hydrogen in Iowa,” Clark said.
Magnetic surveys like what will be conducted in this survery create images of the different magnetic properties carried by different types of rocks, allowing instruments to noninvasively "see" underground.
The Northeaster Iowa and Southwestern Minnesota region being mapped by this survey contains rock types that are magnetic and which may host undiscovered deposits of critical minerals such as nickel, copper, platinum group elements, and cobalt, officials explained in the press release.
Data will be collected along north-south flight lines spaced 1,310 feet (400 meters) apart at a nominal height of 330 feet (100 meters) above ground, increasing to 1,000 feet (300+ meters) above populated areas.
The USGS has contracted with Dewberry and Sander Geophysics Ltd. (SGL) to collect the airborne data. Their fixed-wing aircraft will be equipped with an elongated “stinger” that extends from the main cabin which houses sensors collecting data.
• These scientific instruments are completely passive with no emissions that pose a risk to humans, animals, or plant life.
• No photography or video data will be collected.
• The aircraft will be flown by experienced pilots who are specially trained and approved for low-level flying.
• These pilots work with the FAA to ensure flights are safe and in accordance with U.S. law. The surveys will be conducted during daylight hours only.
Flights will be based out of several regional airports, including Albert Lea, Mason City, and Iowa Falls Airports and fly over parts of 40 counties: Allamakee, Black Hawk, Boone, Bremer, Butler, Cerro Gordo, Chickasaw, Clayton, Fayette, Floyd, Franklin, Greene, Grundy, Hamilton, Hancock, Hardin, Howard, Humboldt, Marshall, Mitchell, Story, Tama, Webster, Winnebago, Winneshiek, Worth, and Wright Counties in Iowa; Blue Earth, Dodge, Faribault, Fillmore, Freeborn, Houston, Mower, Olmstead, Steele, Wabasha, Waseca, and Winona Counties in Minnesota; and Buffalo County in Wisconsin.
Earth MRI includes airborne geophysical surveys like this one, geochemical reconnaissance surveys, topographic mapping using LiDAR technology, hyperspectral surveys, and geologic mapping projects. The data collected are made freely available to the public on the USGS ScienceBase website.
